title: Was life in the Middle Ages really so miserable?
subtitle: Neither short nor dirty
subject: histoire
description: We picture peasants dead at 30, filthy and living on dry bread. Court records, household accounts and skeletons paint a very different portrait.
author: benjamin-campbell

hero.hook: Short lives, dirty bodies, empty stomachs: the archives and the skeletons tell another story.

blocks.text: The Middle Ages have a bad reputation: we imagine people who lived briefly, badly and in filth. One number seems to confirm it, a life expectancy of about **30 years**. It is misleading: that average is dragged down by [[infant mortality]], because so many children died young. It does not mean that most people died before 30.

To understand life more than **1,000 years** ago, historians no longer settle for these statistics. They read court records and household accounts, excavate dwellings and study skeletons. These sources tell how people worked, ate and died. What do they reveal about the daily life of a medieval peasant or townsperson?

Peasants worked hard, but they knew nothing of the Monday-to-Friday week. Farm work followed the **seasons** and the daylight. Sowing and harvest meant long, exhausting days. Winter, by contrast, was much quieter, and many tasks simply waited for the return of fine weather.

blocks.caption: A replica of the Luttrell Psalter (England, c. 1325-1340): the text of the psalms, its margins peopled with small figures.

blocks.text: The [[liturgical calendar]], the calendar of Church feasts, shaped the year too. Sundays and feast days often interrupted ordinary labour: some kinds of work were then paused or forbidden. These breaks did not make peasants a privileged class. Farming remained a gruelling trade, and a poor harvest could put a whole household in danger. But the image of people toiling from sunrise to sunset all year round misses the essential point: medieval work had a rhythm, and that rhythm changed with the months.

For most peasants, an ordinary meal was built around bread and [[pottage]], a thick porridge of grains, often enriched with beans, garden vegetables and scraps of meat. The household also had cheese, eggs and dairy products, all precious sources of protein.

blocks.caption: A baker and his oven in the Tacuinum Sanitatis, an illustrated health handbook of the 14th century.

blocks.text: Meat was certainly eaten, but how often depended on wealth, region and season. **Fish** fed many communities, and preserved vegetables brought variety when fresh produce was scarce. Ale and other fermented drinks were common. The picture of peasants surviving on bread and ale is therefore outdated: what they ate depended on what they could grow, preserve or afford, food that was practical and seasonal rather than monotonous.

Another modern cliché: people who almost never washed. With no plumbing and no bathroom, men and women of the Middle Ages nevertheless cared about cleanliness. **Soap** was used to wash the body as well as linen clothing, and most people washed at home with water from a well or another source.

blocks.caption: A public bath in a manuscript of Valerius Maximus, c. 1470.

blocks.text: In some towns, [[public baths]] were even ordinary places. Collective [[sanitation]], on the other hand, was far worse than today: crowded towns struggled to dispose of their waste, and water was often contaminated. But personal hygiene and public sanitation are two different things. People in the Middle Ages lived alongside dirt; they did not simply accept being dirty.
In some medieval towns, public baths were so numerous that the authorities regulated them and levied a tax on them.

sections.title: A thousand years, a thousand lives

blocks.text: There was no single medieval life. The aristocrat in his stone castle, the peasant on his land and the merchant in a bustling town shared neither the same table, nor the same work, nor the same health. Place and **social rank** decided almost everything, from food to health.

Time mattered just as much. Life in the [[early Middle Ages]], the first centuries after the fall of Rome, was nothing like life in the **14th century**, and conditions in England differed from those on the continent. The period stretched over about **1,000 years** and saw enormous changes in technology, society and politics.

The Middle Ages were therefore not an age of constant hunger, dirt and misery. They were a long period of widely differing lives. Some people lived fairly comfortably on farms or in towns; others faced poverty, disease and an early death. Where and when you lived often counted for more than the label "medieval."
A 30-year life expectancy, filth and dry bread are clichés: medieval daily life depended on place, rank and century far more than on the words "Middle Ages."

sources.text: N. Müller-Scheeßel, C. Rinne et K. Fuchs, « Adult mortality in the metropolis of London 1100-1850: A Bayesian view based on osteological data », American Journal of Biological Anthropology, vol. 185, n° 3, 2024, e25025.
